To address the evolving needs of the data visualization community, the authors propose an extended framework for visual data analysis, incorporating existing and emerging techniques. This framework, based on the existing data flow and visualization layers, also incorporates new knowledge extraction and visualization techniques, such as real-time data processing, machine learning, and more. This new framework, Human-centric Data Visualization, holds promise for a wide range of applications, including remote sensing, where it can address the challenges posed by the rising data volumes.

star and neutron star binary mergers were conducted in 3D general relativity and magnetohydrodynamics to study how magnetic fields in neutron stars are affected.  The study assumed initial merging configurations were relatively symmetric and analyzed black hole accretion disks and remnant neutron stars resulting from the mergers.  Throughout the analysis phases, magnetic fields amplified significantly in the disk and on the remnant neutron star.  After the disintegration of the accretion disk and the stabilization of the magnetic field in the remnant neutron star, this remnant neutron star was found to have magnetic pole strengths of up to 10^14 or even 10^15 gauss.  This remnant neutron star then underwent magnetic field fluctuations and variations in magnetic orientation, eventually leading to the ejection of magnetic fields in magnetic jets.  These magnetic jets were found to have middle pole magnetic strengths of around 10^15 gauss.  It is hypothesized that these magnetic jets may contribute to the generation of fast radio bursts and that these magnetic fields may also be relevant in understanding 1130-year-old supernova remnant G11.  The findings support a possible connection between magnetic fields in neutron stars and Vela pulsars with unique characteristics.

Process model compression reduces the complexity of process models by merging similar activities or states. In this study, we conduct the most comprehensive evaluation of process model compression techniques to date. We compare their effectiveness in EPC and ERC processes, their impact when applied individually or collectively, and their suitability for EPC and ERC processes. kernelization algorithms, are widely employed to demonstrate that instances of decision problems can be solved efficiently when input data exceeds certain thresholds. The standard approach involves reducing instances to a smaller representation, known as a kernel, and storing it entirely in memory. Nevertheless, for instances with exponentially large kernels, such as Vertex Cover, this method proves impractical from a data complexity standpoint. To address this issue, we introduce a novel algorithmic framework that reduces problems with exponentially large kernels in a more memory-efficient manner, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on two graph isomorphism-related issues. Specifically, our method can solve the Vertex Cover decision problem for instances solvable in $O(n \log n)$ time using BSS model, and can run the Le and Vedenev $t$-time algorithm for the Vertex Cover time-dependent problem with $O(\log t)$ space; similarly, we adapt Le and Vedenev's result to the data-complexity model by ensuring both problems take time $2 O(\sqrt{t \log t})$.

a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 spurred researchers to re-examine optical observations made around the time of the merger. This re-analysis revealed the presence of fast-cooling magnetar-like transients within the optical afterglows of the event. In this study, we present an investigation into the characteristics of these transient signals in the GW170817 afterglow. This study reveals the most likely scenario to be neutron star NS1 merging with neutron star NS2 at a distance of 4 Mpc. The collision of these stars gave rise to an ejecta with varying velocity and electron density. The X-ray and optical signals were produced by synchrotron radiation, with particular emphasis on the role of fast-cooling electrons cooling at lower energies. The research reveals that the optical behavior of GW170817 can be effectively described by a rapid initial flash followed by a gradually changing cools period. The research team discovered that the event could be attributed to the merging of two neutron stars, with an alternative possibility being a neutron star merging with a black hole. The central engine's activity in this event can be effectively compared to the kilonovae phenomenon.

Boost have proven effective across various domains. However, these models face a challenge - their lack of interpretability hinders trust in them. To address this issue, various methods have been developed to provide localized approximations that enhance understanding. Despite these efforts, there's a lack of clear guidelines connecting localization methods to interpretability. This study bridges this gap by defining interpretability as the degree of local linearity of a model. By formulating interpretability as the shortest distance to an approximation, we show that existing localization methods don't necessarily minimize this distance. Instead, they implicitly use other approximations, leading to a contrast between local and global errors. This understanding allows us to evaluate the effectiveness of existing methods and guides the development of novel interpretation methods that offer localized confidence intervals.

A previous paraxial approximation yielded a precise $\pi$ phase shift solution that is highly effective when the object's support is known. This approximation is sufficient for CDI when the support encompasses the object's features, but breaks down when the support does not, as the phase of the object extends into its support. Our analysis revolves around three primary questions: Firstly, we seek to understand the thermal properties of these black holes. Our investigation reveals that, at a quantum level, these black holes exhibit two distinct stationary phases. One phase aligns with the traditional black hole behavior, characterized by a singularity-free wormhole geometry, along with the presence of a singularity. A second stationary phase emerges, representing a compact universe with no black hole or wormhole features. Secondly, we investigate the statistical mechanics underlying these phases. Our analysis points to the existence of a unique canonical ensemble that accurately represents the system's thermodynamic attributes. Thirdly, we examine the dynamical processes leading to thermal equilibrium, finding that perturbations within the system decay over time at an exponential rate. Overall, our study offers valuable insight into the interplay between quantum and classical gravitational effects in spherically symmetric polymer black holes.

Specifically, the global data fidelity term of the model is equivalent to the well-known Huber denoising energy, which is a non-local variation removal method. Our research focuses on studying the effects of cosmological expansion on the spectral characteristics of these blazars. These strategies enable the recovery of a blazar's original spectral characteristics despite the apparent distortion caused by the universe's growth.

cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified within a finite sphere of radius. We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, to compute steady-state solutions, from Newtonian infall of particles to relativistic cases with particles given a small initial push. We find that in all cases, particles gain energy and emit radiation that reaches a distant observer. For particles within the event horizon, energy and momentum can be transferred to the black hole and emitted as radiation reaching a distant observer. We find that in finite sphere setups with particles given a small initial push, particles that cross the event horizon lead to thermal radiation with a temperature lower than the Hawking temperature and this does not decrease with larger sphere size. We analyze in detail a simple case of a cloud undergoing non-relativistic infall and present formulas for the energy flux and color temperature seen by a distant observer as the cloud merges with the black hole.

calculate the critical frequency shift of phonons affected by impurities within periodic crystal lattices using the dynamical matrix T-method. The dynamical matrix T represents an underlying trend in the phonon energy spectrum for the pure crystal lattice. By representing impurities as perturbations to this trend, our method identifies the critical frequency shift as the point at which the modified dispersion relation intersects with the trend. This approach enables the precise computation of the phonon-impurity scattering rate without resorting to computationally intensive simulations like molecular dynamics. Moreover, our method reveals that the scattering rate exhibits trend-piezoelectricity dependence, allowing for the exploration of its temperature and defect-strength variations. The results indicate that the scattering rate may decrease by 20% when the temperature drops from 300K to near absolute zero, highlighting the significance of thermal corrections in the T-method. Our dynamical matrix T-method thus represents a groundbreaking development in the computation of phonon-impurity scattering rates, paving the way for the design of novel materials with optimized electronic and thermal properties.

However, traditional RL faces significant limitations when it comes to interacting with people, such as long learning times, uncertain human feedback, and ambiguous success criteria. To address these issues, researchers have turned to asking humans for help when they get stuck during an RL agent's learning process. While this strategy has shown some success, it comes with costs such as distracting people, reducing their understanding, and increasing frustration. To date, RL researchers have not thoroughly explored the trade-offs between requesting human assistance and not when building collaborative RL systems. This paper fills that knowledge gap by introducing the concept of Human Interaction for Reinforcement Learning (HuIRL) to study the interactions between RL agents and humans. Through this study, key questions about when to seek human assistance are identified and a new approach called Human Interaction Help (HiHelp) is introduced. To evaluate the effectiveness of different strategies to request human assistance, the authors developed two new tasks that test various abilities required for real-world robot tasks, such as dealing with uncertainty and adapting to human guidance. The results show that continuous, goal-driven requests for assistance are more effective than one-time or hit-or-miss assistance, as they lead to better collaboration, higher success rates, fewer human interactions, and enhanced overall performance. The researchers plan to make their experimental setup and data available for further study and validation of these findings.

Using neutron diffraction and magnetization measurements, we discovered that CeNiSn exhibits a non-conventional magnetic transition, specifically one that does not result in a clear magnetic order at a critical temperature of 22 mK, but rather forms a glass-like state with continuously changing magnetic configurations. This unusual behavior in the compound's core component (Ce site) contradicts the expectations that a well-established magnetic order would emerge alongside its counterpart (Ni site) magnetic transition. The specific magnetic configurations that arise near 22 mK reveal the presence of very weak magnetic interactions (neighboring magnetic interactions weaker than thermal energy) competing, leading to magnetic rivalry. MA telescopes have uncovered previously unseen radio sources associated with galaxy interactions and mergers. Two of these new objects, found in the Coma Cluster, were not detected by previous surveys. One is associated with an X-ray emitting merger, while the other lies near the margins of the XMM-Coma study area. Although these galaxy interactions may be related to the observed mergers, it's still uncertain if they originate from the most massive galaxies. Further research using optical spectroscopy and radio spectroscopy is required to clarify this relationship. Notably, one of the new objects was found to be associated with a major galaxy in the merger. X-ray analysis suggests that this galaxy interaction occurs approximately 30 million years after its initial collision. This suggests that intense galaxy collisions in the Coma Cluster merger may have given rise to the newly discovered objects. LRFI findings indicate that, in this system, intense galaxy collisions occur at an average rate of once every ten million years in each subsystem until they encounter another intense collision every another 30 million years.

strongly interacting components is challenging, especially when attempting to apply standard statistical methods such as Bayesian approaches. This difficulty arises because typical assumptions for linear and quadratic approximation techniques are not met in such systems. A crucial requirement for implementing Bayesian methods is the availability of a parameter space. Researchers typically introduce this space by making specific assumptions, such as limiting the influence of higher-order interactions, or assume that interactions follow a Gaussian distribution. However, these assumptions may significantly distort the underlying system's behavior, especially when interactions are strong. An alternative approach utilizes machine learning to derive interaction patterns from a given system's configuration Hamiltonian, generating complex interaction maps without relying on simplifying assumptions, thus generating non-Gaussian structures. This study presents an extension of neural network models that can learn to model arbitrary interaction patterns and generates coherent probability distributions over parameters. Furthermore, it develops an efficient algorithm for estimating posterior probabilities, allowing for accurate assessment of the model's predictive capabilities, demonstrated by extensive testing on various tasks, including image classification, block spin analysis, and quantum gauge theories.

A unique property of Weyl semimetal nodes is their inclination to collapse under pressure, temperature changes, or doping. This common characteristic suggests a potential excitonic insulator state in these materials. A theoretical model has been developed to study the phenomenon in 110-oriented SnTe, a material closely related to INSn2Fe16O19, and discovered that in the phase transition process, Weyl nodes transform into electron-hole pockets. This phenomenon was observed through first-principles calculations and is consistent with recent experimental findings, suggesting the possibility of excitonic insulator behavior in this material.

Our goal is to solve this problem with a conservative policy that doesn't break a specified constraint. Our solution involves using an augmented complex state space with a policy augmented constraint. This augmented constraint helps us create a more accurate policy augmented value function. To investigate this arrangement, a new calculation method is developed by applying the green's function Monte Carlo technique within the no-core framework. quantum many-body systems have been achieved through the development of entanglement renormalization methods. However, the quantum many-body problem still poses significant challenges, with entanglement and its intricate behavior being at the heart of these challenges. To address this, entanglement monormalization is introduced as a method for simplifying and decomposing the entanglement structure in quantum many-body systems. Based on a mathematical framework for operator algebra and Heisenberg picture evolution, entanglement monormalization allows a many-body system to be represented as a one-body system through the generation of an effective single-particle Hamiltonian. Effective single-particle Hilbert spaces are also demonstrated to be invariant under time-time correlations and to form vector spaces, which enables the reduction of solving quantum many-body problems to a single-particle Schrödinger equation. As such, efficient computational methods based on time-like correlations can be developed to accurately represent quantum many-body systems. Additionally, entangement monormalization sheds new light on the fundamental representation of quantum many-body systems by reducing their complexity from many-body to single-body systems.

The channel is represented by a double stochastic matrix, where the transition probabilities from the interferenced output to the input and output are both stochastic matrices with identical stationary distributions. As a result, both the input and output processes become Markov processes when transmitted through a finite state channel, enabling a maximum mutual information rate to be achieved. Consequently, the effective capacity of such channels cannot exceed 1 bit per use, as demonstrated in a previous study. However, it has been shown that the effective capacity can approach 1 bit per use, which is not surprising and aligns with expectations. In this work, we provide examples of channels where the effective capacity can be accurately approximated when the number of states is small. Additionally, we provide precise approximations for channels with three states and presented a binary expansion that yields high bounds for this class of channels.

integrated circuit camera sensor into a medical endoscope.  Medical endoscopes are instrumental in various medical examinations and surgical procedures as they facilitate access to restricted body areas.  The current method of capturing images during endoscopic procedures involves connecting an external camera to the patient via a video cable, which then transmits the images to a display unit outside the patient's body.  The displayed images are subsequently recorded and stored separately from the endoscope.  The use of an iCCO, a silicon integrated circuit camera, in medical endoscopes is predicted to enhance image quality, reduce system size, remove the need for external video cables, and allow for the integration of additional medical imaging functions.  The iCCO has the unique capability of on-chip signal processing and thermal management, which sets it apart from other medical imaging technologies.  The iCCO was selected due to its cost-effectiveness, small physical size, customizable pixel configuration, and the ability to package it with a ceramic substrate that provides electrical and thermal insulation.  A prototype of the iCCO was developed based on an analog back-illuminated CMOS technology with 100-micron pixel size and 100kpnF packaging capacitance.  The prototype demonstrated a high frame rate of up to 60 fps at 320x240 resolution with 8-bit dynamic range and B/W color pattern, and passed the standard medical endoscope leak test.

engineers are faced with a significant challenge: reconciling the need for low-latency, high-energy efficiency with the requirement for complex, large-scale data processing operations, which typically require high parallelism and high bandwidth. To address this issue, researchers have developed various architectural solutions, which when combined can be considered a neuromorphic design paradigm. This design is characterized by its use of novel processing elements, simplified algorithms, and a reduced number of spatial and temporal data access operations. However, there have been few implementations that successfully embody this particular paradigm. This work introduces Dataflow-driven Event-based Processing (DEVP), a new hybrid event-data processing architecture designed to tackle the limitations of traditional ANN/DNN and spiking neural network (SNN) designs, which struggle to balance high parallelism and low-latency data access. Implemented on both general-purpose GPUs and custom-built event-data co-processors, the DEVP approach has achieved significant improvements in spatial and temporal efficiency while processing complex data sets.

It is extensively used to address classification issues with time series data, where a standard two-step approach is typically employed: first, extracting features, and then feeding them into machine learning models to generate predictions. Feature extraction methods are often parameterized, which means they require some level of human adjustment to function correctly. To mitigate the impact of features derived from such methods on the overall analysis, research has been conducted to develop selection techniques, such as those based on deep learning. We build upon this research by exploring the effectiveness of end-to-feature learning solutions for classification tasks, where the DTW distance is utilized to measure similarity between time series in a metric learning context. A dataset from a study involving instrument playing is used to evaluate classification results and to compare end-to-feature learning solutions with those that utilize feature selection. Our findings indicate that models trained solely on datasets that mimic the full dataset's distribution can achieve comparable results to those that incorporate an explicit feature selection step.

Although research has been conducted to develop methods for handling missing data, there is limited evidence on how these methods affect machine learning algorithms. This research aims to fill this knowledge gap by comparing machine learning algorithms in supervised binary classification and regression. We evaluate three data insertion methods, including multivariate imputation by chained equations, a random forest-based approach known as knn imputation, and a third method called a mean imputer. Our studyassesses these methods in three scenarios: 1) how machine learning algorithms in supervised binary classification and regression perform with different types of missing data and dataset sizes; 2) how machine learning algorithms perform on test data with missing values; 3) how these methods affect model training and inference speed. Our results show that multivariate imputation by chained equations generally yields better results than other methods in most scenarios.

planets that have been confirmed through the Kepler Space Telescope up to 2016. In total, this includes 129 such planets. Together with existing larger-sample studies, our findings indicate a consistent planet size distribution that peaks at approximately 2.2 Earth radii. Furthermore, this size is largely unaffected by the planet's mass or the depth of the transit that was used to confirm the planet. By comparing our comprehensive dataset with predictions from mass-size relationships, we find that such predictions are only accurate if based on a peak in planet size that is nearly independent of mass. In general, this suggests that using a mass-dependent relationship between size and mass to describe the distribution of super-Earth and sub-Neptune planets is a coincidence. In contrast, if these relationships are formed without considering sizes of smaller planets, they provide a more accurate description of the distribution. By combining observations from transit and atmospheric analysis, we find that planets with smaller sizes tend to have thinner atmospheres, whereas those with thicker atmospheres tend to be larger regardless of mass. In summary, our findings indicate that many planets are likely solid and covered in cool, condensed atmospheres. By removing this feature, our data is best described with a size distribution that peaks at 1.25 Earth radii and grows in mass. This suggests that using a mass-dependent relationship to describe sizes of planets is the best approach.

The distribution was found to be consistent with simulation results. The distribution can be utilized in network modeling.

SARS-CoV-2 in early 2020, has caused a unprecedented crisis and exacerbated existing societal inequalities.  To combat the virus and mitigate social and economic impacts, governments and institutions around the world have implemented restrictive measures.  In response, leaders of scientific communities have initiated projects to accelerate research and promote collaboration, such as the COVID-19 International Supply Chain Initiative (COPISCI) and its related platforms, in an effort to promote transparency and collective problem-solving.  However, these initiatives have been met with challenges and setbacks, highlighting the complexities and limitations of collaborative efforts.  In an attempt to better comprehend and address these challenges, we conducted a thorough examination and analysis of the COPISCI project over its first year and a half.  By gaining insights into its objectives, operations, challenges, and opportunities, we aim to inform and promote more effective strategies for the inclusive and collective management of global health emergencies.  Furthermore, we propose an ideal scientific model for managing international supply chain initiatives, promoting transparency and collective research to mitigate the social and economic impacts of the virus.

Hawking radiation from primordial black holes can be the source currently attributed to the diffuse large-scale structure of the universe we observe today. We aim to rectify this by introducing a novel theoretical framework for non-deterministic network algorithms, focusing on distributed systems where the complicity of an adversary-controlled subset of nodes and links may be at our discretion.  To our knowledge, this complicity can also be compensated by our knowledge.  Our framework offers the ability to define and assess non-deterministic network algorithms, as well as to assess their feasibility in a certifying manner.  In contrast to systems that are deterministic, we suggest a game-theoretic approach, by introducing a co-complicit adversary that attempts to counter our moves in an interactive process.  An algorithm is feasible only if it can overcome any adversary strategy in a game that has a winning condition which is reached within a finite time.  We define in detail the concept of a game theory approach and verify that it is consistent with system verifications, showing that an algorithm which passes verification will win a game against any strategy of the adversary.  We then focus on the case of finite feasibility in terms of messages when verifying an algorithm for finite feasibility against an adversary which is totally complicit.  We prove a significant theorem which establishes the equivalence between these two concepts.  As a practical application, we use this theorem to show that an complictvity compensation mechanism does not lead to significant performance degradation in terms of message complexity.  Finally, we apply this framework to network problems such as Minimum Spanning Trees and Connected Components.

To be detected by current and future sensitivity-enhanced detectors, this memory signal must be separated from the primary waves through advanced analysis techniques like matched filtering or template subtraction. Our research investigates the capabilities of various theoretical models in identifying and characterizing the memory signal within a simulated signal for typical binary black hole collisions. These models are the full general relativity solution approximated for far-field observation, gravitational wave memory approximated through Christodoulou's formula, and a linearized model representing a step change in strain. While all three models are shown to effectively recover key parameters related to spatial-temporal shifts in the memory signal, only the first model yields accurate estimates for the event's distance. Consequently, with present sensitivity levels and a single detection of such an event, obtaining accurate estimates for the shift parameters is feasible, but obtaining accurate estimates for the memory's amplitude is not. However, with future sensitivity levels and a large number of detections by third-generation detectors, obtaining accurate estimates for the amplitude parameter may become possible.

quantum key distribution where a dishonest sender can deliberately exploit imperfections in a real-world direct line to deceive the sender of the secret key into yielding a key that is in real life highly correlated with the infiltrator's information. We present and experimentally test a novel version of our previously proposed method to detect such deception, in which a hidden key's correlation with the infiltrator's information can be accurately assessed in real time using automatically analyzed Bell tests performed on the flying qubits immediately after their transmission. Automatic analysis is necessary due to the inherent instability of the impeding factors in real-world settings. As a result, only continuous and reliably functioning quantum key distribution sessions can be successfully implemented. We successfully integrated this real-life test into a standard quantum key distribution system to dynamically monitor the extent to which the infiltrator's information can possibly obtain about the secret key in real time. We demonstrated that such information can amount to 17% of the key, equivalent to part of the secret key key held by the honest receiver. Meanwhile, through standard tomography of the keying channel, we also determined the level at which the infiltrator can imitate the keying process in real time. We found that our approach offers enhanced robustness against channel interference by allowing key distribution even in situations where traditional distribution methods would fail. We believe our approach paves the way for implementing even more complex real-life quantum protocols with built-in protection against deception, all performed dynamically in real time.

, the sound produced when two rigid bodies collide is a significant aspect. One of the primary challenges in this field is the diffraction effect, which is a complex phenomenon. The diffraction effect, although difficult to model, is the primary obstacle in the virtual sound creation process. Existing research on this topic, including boundary element methods and wave-based approaches, has limitations, such as efficiency and the need for boundary element meshing. The efficiency of the boundary element method is further compromised by its inability to handle an infinite domain, requiring boundary integration. To address these issues, a new model based on boundary element method is proposed, integrating a boundary source term to streamline the process. This model is demonstrated to be capable of introducing body size and shape changes, as well as geometric discontinuities, to synthesize the diffraction effect. The proposed model is validated against the analytical Meehan's model, while an example of changing the body shape and size to modify the sound spectrum is demonstrated.

Research has shown that an optimal sequence of control actions was determined for an environment that takes into account different failure probabilities, thus ensuring that tasks are completed safely and efficiently.

The success of traditional clustering methods relies heavily on the accuracy of their underlying mathematical models, which are designed to describe data generation or system behavior. However, these techniques often fail when encountering real-world, high-dimensional data due to the difficulty in establishing or justifying a suitable mathematical model. As neural networks become integral to clustering algorithms, applying them to systems with no clear mathematical foundation becomes increasingly common. However, it remains unclear how to effectively use neural networks in these scenarios lacking a defined mathematical model. This study explores the effectiveness of different neural network architectures for clustering and discovers that, in instances lacking a clear mathematical model, clustering algorithms based on the underlying graph structure, rather than data-fitting, are the most successful, outperforming those that modify the network to fit the data. The results also indicate that, to achieve satisfactory clustering performance, the chosen architecture needs to be suitable, reflecting insights from both machine learning theory and the broader understanding of neural networks' roles in information processing.

, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums can be investigated through calculations based on a 3+1 lattice framework. Specifically, this involves determining how these medium conditions affect the masses and polarizations of these mesons.

The method utilizes the correlation function ratio approach, incorporating noise-reducing techniques, to derive the meson masses and polarizations from vector-meson dominance model.

Initial findings indicate that the masses and polarizations of rho and phi mesons exhibit changes in local parity violating medium.

For example, the effects of these medium conditions on rho and phi meson masses and polarizations are diverse.

Further, it was discovered that these medium effects diminish as the energy scale increases, and that the effects on rho meson properties are more pronounced than on phi meson properties.

The results are further confirmed by comparing them to existing empirical data.

The study does not yield a complete description of how these medium conditions affect rho and phi meson properties, and it is recommended that a traditional vector-meson dominance model be employed to interpret these results.

The findings also suggest that a more accurate description of local heat effects on meson mass may be needed.

The study also indicates that quantum chromodynamics simulations are necessary to fully understand how these medium conditions affect meson properties.

artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) systems that can make a significant environmental impact has become a key focus for computer scientists. However, the development of these systems often requires the use of computationally intensive and energy-intensive methods, which can have a considerable energy cost. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring the potential of green computing to develop more sustainable and efficient AI/ML systems. Through green AI/ML, the goal is to minimize the energy consumption of these systems while maintaining or even improving their performance. One of the main motivations behind green AI/ML is the scientific inquiry into the trade-offs between a system's efficiency and its energy consumption. To this end, we provide the most comprehensive review to date of green AI/ML, covering the full AI/ML pipeline from preprocessing to model design, ensembles, and boosting, as well as analysis, optimization, training, and training operations. Our review summarizes the current state of green AI/ML by categorizing techniques according to their points of application, identifying the trade-offs involved, and discussing the methods used to evaluate and analyze these green AI/ML techniques. Finally, we highlight the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead in the field of green AI/ML by identifying the key areas of research needed to further the development of this field.

We introduce an alternative hybrid approach, where the algorithm is represented as a sequence of hybrid components, each incorporating an analog operation followed by corrective digital gates, thus enabling the representation of an arbitrary quantum circuit as a single deep analog circuit with interwoven correction steps. We then investigate the origin of these polynomials, outlining their potential uses in understanding and optimizing quantum algorithms in the hybrid digital-analog model.

on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such cases, researchers typically model the dependence using a variance covariance matrix. We have developed a simplified regression-based approach to generate variance covariance matrices that can handle multiple observations per study and provide quick estimates even with a limited number of studies.  This new sense-making approach is based on the concept of pairwise differences, has been found to give results similar to those obtained using more complex fixed or random effects models, and has been applied to 13 studies involving effect sizes that were not independent. The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current methods often struggle to generalise beyond the specific domain in which they are trained.  This issue is particularly pronounced when dealing with environments exhibiting a high level of variance in expert behavior.  This work presents an approach to overcome these limitations, incorporating elements of imitation (expert actions) and replication (agent actions executed by the environment during training).  By leveraging these dual components, the method enables agents to internalise multiple strategies for achieving similar outcomes.  As such, even when these diverse strategies lead to identical objectives, our method produces robust and transferable policies that can be applied across various related domains.  The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through its application to a variety of 2D Tmaze domains and Aerial Navigation tasks.

OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. uncommon to see structures called cavities at a distance of about 5 to 10 astronomical units from the central star, where the intensity of the star's emitted light significantly diminishes. These cavities are thought to be a result of planet-aided disk evolution. A study has been conducted to assess the effectiveness of two common models for how planets interact with these avacities: the model by K69 and the model by TM04. By altering the shape of the cavity and using observations of carbon monoxide and water gas in the disk around the system AB Aur, the transfer of angular momentum between the disk and the planet is better understood. These models produce distinct patterns of heat exchange, and their evaluations suggest that the transfer rate is quite sensitive to the details of the spot. This research allows for new estimates of the amounts of angular momentum exchanged based on the stock of each molecule and their distribution across the spot. Based on the results, the model by TM04 is able to accurately represent the observation of carbon monoxide, but the model for how the planet affects the cavity overestimates the amount of heat exchange, which could lead to evaporation of the water gas. These findings hint at evaporation of the planet that affects the disk and the loss of the dust that builds planets from materials in the spot.

fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the underlying dynamics of events within time series are of significant importance. Traditionally, event modeling relies on parametric distributions' assumptions, yet the development of nonparametric and machine learning-based methods has enabled more versatile approaches, targeting homogeneous events on the basis of inter-arrival times' independence and identical distribution. However, the application of deep learning models' lack of such assumptions has led to their utilization in heterogeneous events analysis, yet their performance is impacted by violations of these assumptions. To overcome these limitations, the exploration of data transformations that preserve the empirical frequency distribution of inter-arrival times and facilitate valid anisotropic event modeling without violations is proposed. As demonstrated through case studies on real-world data applications, the integration of these data transformations enhances the deep learning architecture's interpretability, whereas the focus remains on its application in time-stamped data where event characteristics vary in multiple dimensions.

the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, motion, temperature, mass, chemical composition, and distance. By analyzing the distribution and movement of stars within these structures, we determined that they consist of globular clusters, open clusters, and other stellar formations that were not previously identified. Our research also identified two new examples of structures, referred to as the Eridanus and Phoenix strings. By comparing the kinematics, spatial distribution, and chemical composition of the stars within these structures to those of nearby the Milky Way, we found that they share a common age, low metallicity, and a high degree of similarity to known globular clusters. Our analysis of existing literature and new data from Gaia, including chemical composition data, also revealed that the stars within these structures, particularly the P1 stellar strings, do not share a common origin, as they seem to have both a Galactic and extragalactic origin.

Specifically, we focus on two key limitations: sensitivity to deterministic knife-edge cases and the failure in handling non-existence of unique global optimal solutions. To address these limitations, we leverage concepts from differential geometry and multisection theory in physics. By equating the TD error with the determinant of the Hessian of the TD error, which is influenced by the density of eigenvalue spacing, we ensure that the learning rate and discount factor modulate the weight of different eigenvalues associated with varying temporal scales during learning. This ensures that the algorithm converges toward an equilibrium state with the appropriate discounting of errors, particularly when dealing with characteristics that cannot be optimized. By embedding multisection theory into TD learning, we introduce the Multisection Value Function (MVf), which eliminates the sensitivity to deterministic knife-edge cases and mitigates issues stemming from the non-existence of a unique global optimum. algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context. This paper presents an extended version of the basic unitless recurrent neural networks discussed in our prior research. The theoretical framework of these networks has been proven to guarantee the existence, uniqueness, and stability of their steady states, with the stability determined by the spectral radius of a specific matrix. This theoretical framework enables the construction of a class of cell-based recurrent neural networks that can serve as stable approximations of continuous-time networks. These approximation networks share key mathematical properties with their theoretical counterparts, and their convergence rate is governed by a specific mathematical expression. The validity of these findings has been validated in practice.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), are now capable of achieving state-of-the-art results in computer vision tasks. Despite this success, the high complexity of these models makes them susceptible to adversarial attacks. We investigate the link between DCNN convolutions and semantic image information, and find that subsequent convolutional layers in later networks contain more semantic information. Building on this insight, we propose a later-layer convolutional adversarial example attack method (LLCAE), which targets the refined features in deeper convolutional layers. This approach not only reflects a more state-of-the-the-art understanding of DCNNs but also leads to adversarial examples that are more imperceptible and transferable. Furthermore, we find that LLCAE results in significantly lower distortion levels when applied to image classification networks compared to attacks targeting initial convolutional layers. This is particularly evident when using popular models like ResNet, and places on ImageNet. We substantiate our findings through thorough and state-of-the-art experiments.

Building upon MPI, the Fixed Point Modified Policy Iteration (FPMPI) was developed, which is the contraction fixed point version of MPI and provides an accelerated convergence rate. Concurrent program models incorporating context-switching are required to facilitate model checking of such systems accurately. However, existing implementations often suffer from technical limitations hindering their usability in modern, high-performance computing environments. To address this issue, we propose an improved model checking framework based on the MCMC tool, featuring an enhanced context-switching mechanism enabling the model checking of concurrent programs with context costs. This enhancement allows for the efficient exploration of vast state spaces associated with such systems and facilitates the model checking of concurrent programs using linear memory with context costs. a unique steganography variant known as image steganography, allowing users to conceal confidential messages within seemingly innocuous images shared with other WhatsApp users. Although this technique presents a conflict with the GDPR's requirements for data protection, researchers have found that it actually poses a more severe privacy threat to government officials communicating with civilian populations. Prior investigations into image steganography have yielded mixed results; some revealed that such methods are relatively easy to detect, while others argue that the clandestine messages are often indistinguishable. Surprisingly, it was the assumption that humans can't effectively decode such hidden content - called cryptograms - that we set out to disprove.

What made our approach distinct from earlier studies was our decision to test cryptograms' decodability by actual government employees. We invited six officials from the same district to identify the cryptograms they encountered during their daily interactions. Our findings revealed that not only can these cryptograms be successfully decoded by humans, but also that an array of unconventional techniques are employed in the steganographic process. As a result, it was confirmed that these clandestine messages pose a severe breach of privacy for citizens, thus it is recommended that these officials cease utilizing such methods of communication.

refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, clients apply DBSCAN with variational autoencoders to cluster their local gradients into clean byzantine subgroups. The DBSCAN clusters' centroids are then transmitted to the server, which employs clean centroids to aggregate updates. Both clients and server learn to recognize clusters, with only the cluster identifiers sent to the server to protect user identities. the creation of more convincing deep neural network (DNN)-based voice synthesis. For instance, certain acoustic characteristics such as pitch, timing, and spectral qualities vary depending on emotion.  To achieve this alignment, current systems must accurately deduce these features from the speaker's emotional state.  To address this alignment acoustico-emotional challenge, we've developed an end-to-end technology trained using spoken words expressed across multiple emotions.  Our approach builds on the WaveNet framework.  To match the variations in intonation, rhythmic patterns, and spectral features, we've modified the training objective.  The results show that our technology yields improvements in mean opinion score from 2.71 to 2.93 for different languages, representing some of the highest scores to date, and produces more natural voice samples.  We've also conducted a study where listeners evaluate the alignment of generated voice samples with different emotions.

automatically process and analyze medical images is the need for a large amount of high-quality data, which requires significant time and resources to prepare. Neural Networks (CNNs) are reaching close to human-level performance in various computer vision tasks, yet they struggle with the limitations of nearest-neighbor convolutional grids.  To overcome these constraints, research has been conducted to develop novel convolutional operations that can take the shape of boxes or planes. Specifically, three operations – 3D convolution, max-pooling convolution, and plane convolution – are capable of summarizing data within a given spatial region. In contrast, a newly proposed convolve operation, Convolve3, allows for the controlled spatial pooling of data through the use of a step function. Theoretical analysis confirms that Convolve3 is a generalized version of the above-mentioned operations. Experimentally, our findings show that convolve networks created using this new operation achieve better performance than those based on 3D convolution, max-pooling convolution, and plane convolution.

Objects with non-zero components are referred to as sparse if their non-zero components constitute a small subset of the entire set. These configurations occur frequently in various disciplines such as biology, linguistics, and knowledge representation due to their inherent properties. For instance, species distributions and comment patterns on online platforms are prime examples. Some quantities derived from presence-absence data cannot be simply computed based on individual components and require combining the non-zero components in a more intricate manner. Community metrics in ecology and sparsity-based features in online texts are cases in point. Calculating such complex quantities is often computationally demanding, particularly when dealing with large datasets. Introducing a newly proposed algorithm allows for faster computation of specific metrics like the Sørensen-Dice coefficient, also seen in the Jaccard index, for many sparse objects at once, enabling results to be computed linearly in the total number of non-zero components. Our experimental analysis confirms the efficiency of the algorithm and outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches for exact solutions, then approximates its performance with novel hierarchical and parallel methods.

in the diagnosis and treatment planning of head injuries, particularly traumatic brain injury. An essential aspect involves the non-invasive assessment of intracranial pressure, which can be achieved by analyzing CT scans. Current research has relied on two-dimensional, axial slices for this purpose. In this study, we utilized three-dimensional, raw CT scan data to develop an in-vivo model that estimates intracranial pressure by analyzing the internal brain structure. This was achieved by segmenting the brains of 1,000 patients with varying levels of intracranial pressure, resulting in 3D models with accurately classified Brain, Skull, and Air spaces. Our subsequent analysis used statistical shape modeling to analyze these segments, which was then integrated with pressure data to determine the relationship between the internal brain structure and intracranial pressure. Our evaluation, based on leave-one-out cross-validation, demonstrated an average mean absolute error of 9.8 mmHg compared to other studies with 2D, axial image data. Our methodology paves the way for developing advanced, three-dimensional image analysis tools for diagnosing traumatic brain injury.

models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, with the U(1)X symmetry defined by two parameters. The parameters determine the gauge couplings of all fermions, including the three types of neutrinos. By combining these U(1)X models with the Fermi-Siegel symmetry, we obtain models that include the Majorana mass terms for right-handed neutrinos with no or one generation flavor. The Fermi-Siegel symmetry ensures that the Standard Model's accidental symmetries are fully recovered. Furthermore, we prove that the parameters defining the gauge couplings must adhere to specific relationships in order to produce realistic models. These relationships facilitate the construction of a realistic model through the Fermi-Siegel symmetry mechanism. The Higgs and right-handed neutrino sectors of this U(1)X framework are capable of producing a type-I neutrino mass mechanism and a realistic lepton flavor violation pattern.

the mechanical characteristics of millimeter-thin, single-crystal silicon wafers with varying crystal orientations, as it produces distinct sound patterns when under stress. These wafers exhibit unique stress patterns based on their crystal orientation, making it possible to identify them through acoustic analysis. Two methods were developed for measuring the mechanical wave speeds in such wafers, involving the excitation and detection of stress patterns through the surface of the wafer. One method, time-domain surface wave reflection (TDSR), involves analyzing stress patterns following a sudden impact, while time-domain sinusoidal wave reflection (TDSWR) involves sending out smooth waves at various frequencies and depths. Two experiments were conducted, involving wafers with different crystal orientations and an additional test using an x-ray method to validate the results. The experiments used a device for measuring the stress of the wafers and two methods for measuring mechanical wave speeds for comparison. The results showed agreement between theoretical and experimental findings for both experimental methods used.

In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from post-selection methods, which are characterized by high experimental complexity, limited efficiency, and intrusive properties. In this research, a more efficient approach is proposed, which is based on a novel type of entanglement called hyper-entangled state. By leveraging this concept, we can create polarization entanglement without relying on post-selection, using only genuinely quantum resources. The novel approach has significant practical implications as it can be applied in quantum communication, precision measurements, fundamental tests, and other related scientific fields.

critical requirement, especially in the context of security. The security status of an IoT device heavily depends on its operating system. Consequently, accurately identifying the operating system of an IoT device is a crucial prerequisite for effective security enforcement. In this research, we have developed DT-IoT-DSC, a device signature and categorization framework tailored for IoT traffic. DT-IoT-DSC learns device signatures by analyzing communication patterns and associated temporal behavior. These devices are then grouped into different categories based on their similarities. Building upon these established categories, DT-IoT-DSC employs a trained decision tree model to accurately infer device signatures and perform device classification. Our results indicate that DT-IoT-DSC can accurately infer device characteristics and perform multi-device classification with accuracies of up to 98.8% and 94.0%, respectively.

To bridge this gap, we have developed a novel interpretation of Hebbian learning that aligns with the principles of adaptive brain function. Our approach is grounded in thermodynamics and the integration of Gibbs variables, which govern the process of adaptive learning. By applying a continuous-time discrete event algorithm to integrate Gibbs differentials, we have formulated a computationally feasible version of Hebbian learning. Our framework provides multiple, compatible implementations of Hebbian learning that are rooted in adaptive principles. To demonstrate the practical application of our approach, we have developed a brain model that we apply to train a robot to navigate a complex 3D environment. Our results show that the robot's navigation speed and efficiency are comparable to those of a robot trained using traditional, non-adaptive Hebbian learning. Additionally, our approach enables us to quantify the efficiency of the Hebbian process and the efficiency of its controller. Our findings also suggest that our alignment of adaptive principles and Hebbian learning opens the door to the evolution of ecological laws within the biological realm.

how living beings interact with their surroundings. It assumes that the brain constructs a model, or 'predictive coding', of the environment to anticipate sensory input. our investigation focuses on how much information a noiseless channel can convey under specific correlation constraints with the source. We establish an upper limit on the entropy of the output from this channel, denoted as $Y$, given its input $X$ and subject to the condition that it is compatible with the original channel's output $Z$ and satisfies $I(X;Z)=0$. The derived bound shows that the entropy can be limited by the sum of the mutual information between $X$ and $Z$ and the minimum possible entropy of $Y$ given $Z$. The proof involves constructing a novel channel that combines the minimum non-degenerate channel and the original channel in an equivalent way, thereby yielding an upper limit on the entropy of combined channels. The notion of combining non-degenerate channels is defined for the first time in this investigation and is shown to satisfy certain key properties. The provided bound suggests the existence of conditional minimum non-degenerate channels that generalize the concept of minimal non-degenerate channels and are useful in analyzing source coding under constrained error conditions. The given framework may have potential applications in source coding under constrained error conditions, channel simulation, and related areas.

Within this context, nonextensive statistics offer a means of addressing challenges that arise when dealing with systems characterised by interaction-dependent forces that diverge from standard power laws. By employing nonextensive mechanics, the impact of interaction-dependent correlation functions on nonextensivity parameters can be quantified, thereby providing a unified approach to addressing systems of interactive particles. However, it is essential to note that nonextensive mechanics is not the sole method of addressing interactive forces; alternative approaches, such as density-dependent interaction potentials, can also be used to model interaction effects, which may lead to nonextensivity under specific conditions. The objective of the present work is to compare the outcomes of nonextensive mechanics with those of density-dependent interaction potentials, as well as examine their compatibility, which can be demonstrated by modifying the interaction phase space measure in the case of Tsallis' framework, which can be effectively merged with a position-dependent nonextensive interaction. The results are then compared with the cases of standard Boltzmann-Gibbs mechanics and noninteracting systems, which serve as limiting cases.

a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems that draw from multiple neural networks.  The course draws on theoretical and experimental research to explore how the human brain's information processing capabilities can be harnessed to create more advanced artificial intelligence systems.  The instructors for this course are Andrew B. Goldberg and Samuel R..  Gershman.
=== L1: Introducing the dynamic inventory model of neural resource allocation ===
The dynamic inventory model of neural resource allocation is an innovative approach to understanding how the brain's neurons work together to store and retrieve information over time.  The course delves into how this model can inform the design of neural interfaces for locked-in syndrome and other conditions that affect human communication.
=== L2: The role of the prefrontal cortex in cognitive control ===
The prefrontal cortex plays a central role in the design of intelligent systems, making it essential to understand its function.  The course introduces key principles of cognitive control and how the prefrontal cortex is involved in learning to use these principles to solve complex problems.
